This draft is organized to mirror the pedagogical arc that made classic CS texts durable: from primitives, to interpreters, to systems, to society.

Throughline

The central claim of this project is that agentic AI is a science of interaction and orchestration, not merely API plumbing. We seek principles that are testable, compositional, and programmable.

Goals, Environments, and Actions

Every agent story begins like an old sea tale: fog everywhere, limited instruments, and one irretrievable move at a time. If we cannot say what counts as “north,” what currents the world obeys, and which moves are legal, then we do not have an agent architecture yet—we have charisma and wishful thinking. The disciplined alternative is to specify goals, environment dynamics, and action semantics so that behavior can be analyzed, improved, and held accountable [2].

Running example: a coding agent under deadline

Imagine a coding agent tasked with shipping a bug fix before a release freeze. Its goal is not “write something clever,” but maximize expected task value (tests pass, regression risk low, deadline met). Its environment includes a partially observed repository state, flaky CI, and hidden downstream dependencies. Its actions include reading files, editing code, running tests, and opening a pull request. At each step it sees only a slice of the truth, chooses one action, and changes the very world it must reason about next [3] [7].

Formal model (and how it maps to code)

Let the agent-environment system be [ \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{A},T,\Omega,R,C,\gamma), ] where (\mathcal{S}) is latent state, (\mathcal{O}) observations, (\mathcal{A}) actions, (T(s'\mid s,a)) transition dynamics, (\Omega(o\mid s,a)) observation dynamics, (R) reward, (C) constraint costs, and (\gamma\in(0,1)) discount [4] [7] [51].

A policy (\pi(a\mid h_t)), with history (h_t=(o_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})), solves the constrained objective [ \max_{\pi}\;J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}{\pi,T,\Omega}!\left[\sum\gamma^t R(s_t,a_t)\right] \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \mathbb{E}}^{\infty{\pi}!\left[\sum\gamma^t C_j(s_t,a_t)\right]\le\kappa_j\;\forall j. ] Natural-language prompts are therefore only the front door; the house is built from explicit (R), (C), and stopping criteria.}^{\infty

A practical Python mapping might look like this:

Formal symbol Meaning Typical Python field
(\mathcal{O}, o_t) observations AgentStep.observation
(\mathcal{A}, a_t) admissible and chosen actions AgentSpec.action_space, AgentStep.action
(R(s_t,a_t)) task utility signal AgentStep.reward
(C(s_t,a_t)) safety/budget costs AgentStep.costs
(T,\Omega) world and sensing models WorldModel.transition(), WorldModel.observe()
(\pi(a\mid h_t)) decision rule Policy.select_action(history)

When these fields are explicit, “agent behavior” stops being mystical and becomes inspectable engineering.

Three-theory braid

Expected-utility theory gives us the compass by declaring that rational choice under uncertainty is to pick (a^\star) maximizing (\sum_s P(s\mid a)U(s)), so preference becomes computation rather than rhetoric [33] [34]; sequential decision theory then warns that single-step cleverness is a trap because each move reshapes tomorrow’s opportunity set, captured by (V^\star(s)=\max_a{R(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}T(s'\mid s,a)V^\star(s')}) and, under partial observability, by belief updates (b_{t+1}(s')=\eta\,\Omega(o_{t+1}\mid s',a_t)\sum_s T(s'\mid s,a_t)b_t(s)), which force planning over information as well as outcomes [4] [5] [7]; and feedback control finally keeps this entire edifice honest by insisting that plans must survive noisy reality through closed loops such as (x_{t+1}=Ax_t+Bu_t+w_t), (y_t=Cx_t+v_t), and corrective control (u_t=-K\hat{x}_t), with state estimation continuously updating (\hat{x}_t) from observations, so intelligence is not perfect prediction but graceful correction under disturbance [36] [39] [41].

Short exercise

Take a real prompt you use (for example, “Refactor this module safely and quickly”) and formalize it as ((R,C,\text{termination})): define one reward term for functional correctness, one for latency or token cost, at least one hard safety constraint, and a measurable stopping condition. Then write one sentence explaining which part of your spec corresponds to utility, dynamics, and feedback.

How to study this formally

Build small benchmark tasks where (R) and (C) are explicit, perturb observations and transition assumptions, and compare policies by constrained return, regret, and violation rate. If a system cannot state its objective and constraints mathematically, it may still be impressive—but it has not yet earned the full title of agent.

Belief, Uncertainty, and Decision

The competent agent does not pray for certainty; it budgets uncertainty like an engineer with a deadline and a power bill. In serious systems, belief is not a vibe, not a slogan, and definitely not a confidence emoji—it is a state variable that must earn its keep in every action you take.

Bayesian formalization

Let (s_t) be latent world state, (h_t=(o_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})) be history, and (b_t(s)=P(s_t=s\mid h_t)) be the agent's belief. Under a POMDP model, belief evolves by Bayesian filtering [7] [4]: [ b_{t+1}(s')=\eta\,\Omega(o_{t+1}\mid s',a_t)\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}T(s'\mid s,a_t)b_t(s), ] with (\eta) as normalization. The observation model also gives a posterior predictive law, [ P(o_{t+1}\mid b_t,a_t)=\sum_{s'}\Omega(o_{t+1}\mid s',a_t)\sum_s T(s'\mid s,a_t)b_t(s), ] which is the agent's explicit wager about what reality will show next. Decision quality is then evaluated in belief space: [ V^\pi(b)=\mathbb{E}!\left[\sum_{t\ge 0}\gamma^t R(s_t,a_t)\mid b_0=b,\pi\right]. ] At each step, the normative move is expected-utility maximization [33] [34]: [ a_t^\star=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}[U(a,S_t)\mid h_t]. ]

Worked example: heuristic bravado vs Bayesian humility

Suppose an agent chooses between Shortcut (A) and Detour (B), while weather (S\in{\text{clear},\text{storm}}) is hidden. Utilities are (U(A,\text{clear})=10), (U(A,\text{storm})=-20), and (U(B,\text{clear})=U(B,\text{storm})=4). A deterministic heuristic ("always pick the shorter route") commits to (A), yielding [ \mathbb{E}[U(A)]=0.5(10)+0.5(-20)=-5. ] Bayesian control first asks for a forecast (q) with (90\%) accuracy. If (q=\text{clear}), then (P(\text{clear}\mid q=\text{clear})=0.9) and [ \mathbb{E}[U(A)\mid q=\text{clear}]=0.9(10)+0.1(-20)=7>4=\mathbb{E}[U(B)\mid q=\text{clear}], ] so take (A). If (q=\text{storm}), then (P(\text{clear}\mid q=\text{storm})=0.1) and [ \mathbb{E}[U(A)\mid q=\text{storm}]=0.1(10)+0.9(-20)=-17<4, ] so take (B). Same roads, same world, radically different policy quality—because one agent updates.

Information as an economic action

Information gathering is not a prelude to action; it is an action with cost, latency, and opportunity cost. The value of information for query (q) is [ \operatorname{VoI}(q)=\mathbb{E}!\left[\max_a \mathbb{E}[U(a,s)\mid h_t,q]\right] \;-\;\max_a \mathbb{E}[U(a,s)\mid h_t]. ] In the toy route problem, without querying we choose (B) for utility (4). With the forecast, expected utility is [ 0.5\cdot 7 + 0.5\cdot 4 = 5.5, ] so (\operatorname{VoI}=5.5-4=1.5). If the API call costs (0.8) utility units (time, tokens, dollars), net gain is (0.7): query first, act second. If the call cost were (2), the same "more information!" instinct would be irrational.

Three-theory braid

Bayesian decision theory tells us to choose (a^\star=\arg\max_a \mathbb{E}[U(a,S)\mid h]), information theory tells us how much ignorance remains via (H(S\mid h)=-\sum_s b(s)\log b(s)) and how much a query might retire via (I(S;Q\mid h)=H(S\mid h)-H(S\mid h,Q)), and sequential control tells us that these local choices compound through Bellman structure (V^\star(b)=\max_a{r(b,a)+\gamma\sum_o P(o\mid b,a)V^\star(\tau(b,a,o))}), so the agent is not merely selecting an action but selecting the future quality of its own epistemic state [34] [35] [5] [7]; in deployed systems this braid closes the loop through estimation and control—state estimate (\hat{x}_t) from filtering, then feedback (u_t=-K\hat{x}_t)—which is the practical reminder that uncertainty is not an academic footnote but the very signal driving closed-loop behavior [36] [41].

When approximate inference is acceptable

Exact Bayesian filtering is often too expensive for production loops, so approximation is acceptable when it is decision-safe, not merely statistically pretty. Define the action gap [ \Delta(b)=Q(b,a^\star)-\max_{a\ne a^\star}Q(b,a), ] and suppose approximation yields (\tilde Q) with uniform error (\lvert \tilde Q(b,a)-Q(b,a)\rvert\le \varepsilon_Q). Then the greedy action is unchanged whenever [ \Delta(b)>2\varepsilon_Q. ] This gives a practical criterion: particle filters, variational approximations, or distilled surrogates are fine when they preserve action ranking where it matters, stay calibrated under proper scoring rules, and respect latency budgets [37] [38] [49].

How to study this formally

Run ablations where retrieval, tool probes, and clarification questions are explicit costly actions; then report downstream utility, realized (\operatorname{VoI}), and calibration (e.g., Brier score (BS=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (p_i-y_i)^2)) under matched latency/token budgets [49]. If epistemic actions do not improve calibrated decision quality per unit cost, your agent is performing epistemology theater—dramatic, expensive, and mostly decorative.

World Models and State Abstractions

A world model is a map drawn during a storm: if you sketch every raindrop, you never choose a road; if you sketch only the horizon, you drive into a lake. State abstraction is that disciplined cartography—selective forgetting in service of competent action, where elegance is measured not by compression ratio alone, but by whether the agent still reaches the right future.

Formalization

Let the ground control problem be an MDP ((\mathcal S,\mathcal A,T,R,\gamma)) [4] [5], and let (\phi:\mathcal S\to\mathcal Z) be an abstraction map. Exact homomorphism requires reward and transition consistency [37]: [ R(s,a)=\bar R(\phi(s),a),\qquad \sum_{s':\phi(s')=z'}T(s'\mid s,a)=\bar T(z'\mid \phi(s),a). ] Then planning may occur in the compressed space via [ \bar V^{}(z)=\max_{a\in\mathcal A}\Big[\bar R(z,a)+\gamma\sum_{z'}\bar T(z'\mid z,a)\bar V^{}(z')\Big], ] and the lifted policy (\pi(s)=\bar\pi(\phi(s))) preserves optimal control structure in the original system [37]. In approximate abstractions, if reward and transition mismatches are bounded by (\varepsilon_R) and (\varepsilon_P), a standard simulation-style bound is [ |V^{}-\bar V^{}!\circ\phi|\infty \lesssim \frac{\varepsilon_R}{1-\gamma}+\frac{\gamma R\varepsilon_P, ] which makes the central bargain explicit: every saved byte must pay rent in decision quality [}}{(1-\gamma)^237] [39].

Bisimulation metrics refine this bargain by turning “close enough” into geometry [38]: [ d(s,s')=\max_{a\in\mathcal A}\Big(|R(s,a)-R(s',a)|+\gamma\,W_d\big(T(\cdot\mid s,a),T(\cdot\mid s',a)\big)\Big), ] with (W_d) the Kantorovich lift induced by (d). If (d(s,s')) is small, the states are behaviorally interchangeable up to a quantified tolerance.

And because agents act on worlds rather than merely describing them, causal world models encode mechanism, not just association [6]: [ X_i=f_i(\mathrm{Pa}(X_i),U_i),\qquad P(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_i P(x_i\mid \mathrm{pa}i), ] while intervention semantics replace observation with surgery: [ P(x_1,\dots,x_n\mid \mathrm{do}(X_j=x))=\mathbf{1}[x_j=x]\prod_i). ] That is the mathematical line between “I saw this happen” and “I can make this happen.”}P(x_i\mid \mathrm{pa

Code-facing pattern: logs are archives, state is policy fuel

A practical pattern is to separate observation logs (high-volume, append-only) from decision state (small, control-sufficient summary):

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class AgentMemory:
    event_log: list[dict]          # full transcript / telemetry archive
    decision_state: dict           # compact features used by planner


def ingest(observation: dict, mem: AgentMemory) -> AgentMemory:
    mem.event_log.append(observation)
    mem.decision_state = update_belief(mem.decision_state, observation)
    return mem


def act(mem: AgentMemory):
    return policy(mem.decision_state)

Use the log for audit and targeted retrieval, but let the policy read only (z_t=\psi(h_t)), a compressed sufficient statistic. In Chapter 2’s memory controller framing (see Memory Systems, Context, and Retrieval), retrieval should be a gated action with explicit cost, not an always-on reflex.

Cautionary case: when memory abundance became planning starvation

One common failure mode is transcript maximalism: define state as (s't=(s_t,\ell_t)), where (\ell_t) is a long raw interaction log, then wonder why planning quality collapses. The planner now optimizes over irrelevant detail, value estimates become noisier, and action ranking destabilizes under tiny prompt perturbations. Formally, the right requirement is conditional sufficiency, [ P(s,r_t\mid z_t,a_t),\qquad z_t=\psi(h_t), ] not archival completeness. If your state remembers everything except what the next decision needs, you have built a luxury memory palace with no steering wheel.},r_t\mid h_t,a_t)=P(s_{t+1

Three-theory braid

State abstraction tells us how to compress without lying to control, bisimulation metrics tell us exactly how much behavioral truth was lost in that compression, and causal modeling tells us whether the compressed model still answers intervention questions rather than merely replaying correlations; together they define a disciplined pipeline in which action is still chosen by expected utility (a_t^{}=\arg\max_a\mathbb E[U(a,S_t)\mid z_t]) [34], long-horizon consequences are propagated through Bellman recursion (V^{}(z)=\max_a{\bar R(z,a)+\gamma\sum_{z'}\bar T(z'\mid z,a)V^{*}(z')}) [5] [39], and execution closes the loop through feedback laws such as (u_t=-K\hat x_t), where estimation and control co-govern real behavior [36] [41]; the moral is wonderfully unforgiving: a useful world model must be compact enough to think with, faithful enough to plan with, and causal enough to intervene with, or else the agent remains a brilliant spectator of consequences it cannot reliably shape [37] [38] [6].

How to study this formally

Benchmark abstractions by (i) value loss (\Delta_V=|V^{}-\tilde V^{}\circ\phi|_\infty), (ii) intervention fidelity gaps on counterfactual test sets (compare (P(Y\mid \mathrm{do}(X=x))) predictions to observed outcomes), and (iii) robustness under distribution shift when retrieval budgets are constrained. Then run an ablation where you increase raw memory exposure while holding task and compute fixed; if extra memory hurts return, your agent is not under-informed—it is over-narrated.

Policies, Value, and Control

A policy is not merely “what the model says next”; it is the constitution of an artificial polity under uncertainty, delay, and temptation. If goals are the crown and actions are the ministers, policy is the legal code that keeps cleverness from mutiny.

Core equations

Let (\pi(a\mid s)) be a policy over an MDP. The long-run bookkeeping is value: [ V^\pi(s)=\mathbb{E}\pi!\left[\sum\gamma^t r_t\mid s_0=s\right],\qquad Q^\pi(s,a)=\mathbb{E}}^{\infty\pi!\left[\sum\gamma^t r_t\mid s_0=s,a_0=a\right]. ] Bellman recursion turns this into a compositional law of consequence [}^{\infty5] [39]: [ V^{}(s)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left{R(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in\mathcal{S}}T(s'\mid s,a)V^{}(s')\right}. ] At one step, decision-theoretic choice is expected utility [33] [34]: [ a_t^{*}=\arg\max_a\;\mathbb{E}[U(a,S_t)\mid h_t]. ] With parameterized policies, adaptation follows the policy-gradient theorem [40]: [ \nabla_\theta J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}{\pi\theta}!\left[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\,Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)\right], ] and often uses the advantage baseline [ A^\pi(s,a)=Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s) ] to reduce variance without changing the expected gradient [3] [40].

A failure case: brilliant proposal, absent oversight

Consider a coding agent choosing between FastPatch and SafePatch before a production freeze. The proposal policy has superb local instincts and estimates [ \hat Q(s,\text{FastPatch})=9.2,\qquad \hat Q(s,\text{SafePatch})=7.4, ] so without governance it ships FastPatch every time. But the real system is constrained: [ \max_\pi\;\mathbb{E}\pi!\left[\sum\gamma^t r_t\right] \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \mathbb{E}\pi!\left[\sum\gamma^t c_t\right]\le \kappa, ] and FastPatch quietly violates a hard safety budget (auth bypass risk, rollback blast radius), yielding high short-term reward and catastrophic tail cost [51] [53]. Capability, unguided, became a speedrun into policy debt.

Proposal/adjudication/oversight composition (pseudo-code)

function ACT(state x_t, history h_t):
    candidates <- ProposePolicy.sample_actions(x_t, h_t, K)

    # Adjudication: optimize task value under soft risk penalty
    for a in candidates:
        value[a] <- V_hat(x_t, a)
        risk[a]  <- C_hat(x_t, a)
        score[a] <- value[a] - lambda * risk[a]
    a_star <- argmax_a score[a]

    # Oversight: enforce hard constraints before execution
    if violates_hard_constraints(x_t, a_star):
        a_safe <- OversightPolicy.fallback(x_t, h_t)   # safe default / escalate
        return a_safe

    return a_star

This split does something monoliths rarely do: it lets imagination be bold, judgment be quantitative, and governance be stubborn.

Value estimation is not confidence scoring

Value estimation asks, “If I take this action, how much discounted utility should I expect?” Confidence scoring asks, “How sure am I that my prediction or label is correct?” They are cousins, not twins. Formally, [ \hat V(s)\approx \mathbb{E}!\left[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t r_t\mid s\right] ] is about outcome magnitude, while a confidence model outputs [ \hat p(y\mid x)\approx P(Y=y\mid X=x) ] and is judged by calibration metrics such as Brier score [ \mathrm{BS}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (p_i-y_i)^2 ] [49]. An action can have high confidence and low value (certainly safe but useless), or lower confidence and high value (risky but worth it); policy quality depends on expected utility, not swagger.

Three-theory braid

Dynamic programming gives the grammar of optimality through Bellman structure, where every present act is a price tag on future possibility (V^{}(s)=\max_a{R(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}T(s'\mid s,a)V^{}(s')}) [5] [39]; policy-gradient learning then supplies adaptation when models are partial and function approximation is unavoidable, nudging parameters by (\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)]) so control laws can learn from experience instead of scripture [40] [3]; and model predictive control operationalizes this in the unruly present by repeatedly solving a finite-horizon constrained optimization, executing the first move, re-measuring reality, and replanning, with feedback law intuition captured by forms like (u_t=-K\hat x_t), so expected utility (a^{*}=\arg\max_a\mathbb{E}[U(a,S)\mid h]) becomes not a one-shot maxim but an institutional loop in which proposing, deciding, and policing co-evolve under uncertainty, constraints, and disturbance [34] [41] [51] [52].

How to study this formally

Evaluate layered policies with ablations: proposer-only, proposer+adjudicator, and full proposer+adjudicator+oversight. Report constrained return, violation rate, closed-loop stability indicators, and calibration of risk/confidence heads under matched latency budgets. If the “smartest” policy wins only when constraints are ignored, you have not built control—you have built a very articulate gamble.

Reasoning Loops as Interpreters

An agent loop is an interpreter wearing orchestration clothing. Once we say this out loud, semantics, invariants, and proofs become available to us.

Small-step semantics

Define machine state (\sigma=(m, h, b, \tau)): memory (m), interaction history (h), belief state (b), and tool context (\tau).
Transitions are relations (\sigma \xrightarrow{\ell} \sigma') labeled by step kind (\ell \in {\texttt{think},\texttt{act},\texttt{observe},\texttt{reflect}}).

An agent loop is the least fixed point of a transition functional: [ \mathcal{L}(\sigma)= \begin{cases} \sigma & \text{if }\texttt{halt}(\sigma)\ \mathcal{L}(F(\sigma)) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} ] where (F) is one semantic step.

Three-theory braid

  1. Structural operational semantics (SOS). Behavior is specified via transition rules, making legal/illegal steps explicit [42].
  2. Abstract interpretation. We reason soundly about large state spaces using abstract domains and transfer functions [43].
  3. Reason-act coupling in LLM agents. ReAct-style trajectories instantiate interpreter steps over tool-mediated environments [11].

How to study this formally

Prove step invariants (schema validity, budget monotonicity), termination conditions, and recovery properties from error states. If you cannot define your loop semantics, you cannot debug your loop semantics; you can only squint at transcripts and hope.

Deliberation, Planning, and Search

Deliberation is the art of spending computation now to avoid regret later.

Formal planning frame

Let (G=(V,E)) be a search graph over decision states. A plan is a path (p=(v_0,\dots,v_T)) minimizing [ J(p)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} c(v_t,v_{t+1}) + \Phi(v_T), ] with admissible heuristic (h(v)\le h^{}(v)) for A optimality.

In stochastic domains, planning becomes belief-space optimization or Monte Carlo tree search over sampled rollouts.

Three-theory braid

  1. Heuristic graph search. A* gives optimality guarantees under admissibility/consistency assumptions [8].
  2. Symbolic planning. STRIPS-style operators and planning-domain models encode action preconditions/effects for compositional plan construction [9] [10].
  3. Anytime and tree-search control. UCT/MCTS and anytime planning trade compute for solution quality under real-time budgets [44] [45].

How to study this formally

Benchmark plan quality against compute budget, replan frequency, and irreversible-error rate. Analyze sensitivity to heuristic misspecification and environment volatility. The best planner is not the one with the fanciest tree; it is the one whose assumptions fail gracefully.

Memory Systems, Context, and Retrieval

Memory is policy, not pile: retain, compress, retrieve, forget. The trick is to optimize this policy under context-window scarcity.

Formal memory policy

Let memory state be (m_t=(w_t,e_t,s_t)): working, episodic, and semantic stores.
A memory controller chooses operations (u_t \in {\texttt{write},\texttt{compress},\texttt{retrieve},\texttt{evict}}) by [ u_t = \mu_\theta(m_t,h_t), ] to optimize [ \max_\mu\ \mathbb{E}!\left[\sum_t \gamma^t \big(\text{task_utility}_t - \lambda_1\text{latency}_t - \lambda_2\text{token_load}_t\big)\right]. ]

Three-theory braid

  1. Cognitive multi-store theory. Distinct working/episodic/semantic strata suggest principled architectural separation [48].
  2. Information-theoretic compression. Retention is a rate-distortion tradeoff: keep bits that preserve decision value [35].
  3. Modern retrieval theory. Sparse/dense indexing and RAG latent-document models define end-to-end evidence pipelines [14] [15] [46] [47].

How to study this formally

Evaluate retrieval precision/recall, downstream answer faithfulness, and regret from memory eviction decisions. Stress-test long-horizon tasks with adversarial distractors. If memory policy cannot be audited quantitatively, “long context” is just expensive amnesia.

Evaluating and Debugging Reasoners

If you only score final answers, you reward lucky shortcuts and miss systematic failure. Reasoners must be judged as stochastic processes over trajectories.

Formal evaluation object

Let trajectory (\tau=(\sigma_0,a_0,\dots,\sigma_T)\sim p_\pi(\tau)).
Define task utility (U(\tau)), safety cost (C(\tau)), and calibration score (S(\tau)).
Evaluation is multi-objective: [ \max_\pi \ \mathbb{E}[U(\tau)] - \lambda\,\mathbb{E}[C(\tau)] \quad\text{with calibration constrained by}\quad \mathbb{E}[S(\tau)] \le \epsilon. ]

Three-theory braid

  1. Proper scoring rules. Calibration and probabilistic honesty are measured with strictly proper losses (e.g., log score, Brier) [49].
  2. Trace-based causal diagnosis. Interventional replay and counterfactual edits reveal which loop step caused failure [6].
  3. Influence-based debugging. Influence-function approximations identify training/data points or memory entries that drive specific errors [50].

How to study this formally

Instrument every loop step, replay with controlled interventions, and report confidence-utility frontiers rather than single accuracy points. A reasoning stack graduates from demo to system only when its failures are reproducible, attributable, and reducible.

Tool Interfaces and Function Calling

Tool use is where language stops narrating and starts doing. The central artifact is not the prompt—it is the contract.

Formal contract model

Represent tool (f) by [ f : X \to Y,\quad \text{with } \texttt{Pre}f(x),\ \texttt{Post}_f(x,y),\ \texttt{Cost}_f(x),\ \texttt{Risk}_f(x). ] An invocation is legal iff (\texttt{Pre}_f(x)=\texttt{true}).
A planner selects tool call (u_t=(f_t,x_t)) by maximizing expected utility under cost/risk constraints: [ u_t^{*} = \arg\max(u). ]} \ \mathbb{E}[Q(\sigma_t,u)] - \lambda_c \texttt{Cost}(u) - \lambda_r \texttt{Risk

Three-theory braid

  1. Schema-typed interfaces. Function-calling schemas convert natural-language intent into machine-checkable arguments [13].
  2. Self-supervised tool-use learning. Toolformer-style training demonstrates that models can internalize tool-selection policies from weak supervision [12].
  3. Compositional action semantics. Reason-act trajectories make tool calls first-class state transitions suitable for replay and policy improvement [11].

How to study this formally

Track precondition violation rate, postcondition success, rollback frequency, and utility gain per call. A tool interface is mature when failures are classifiable by contract violation rather than “the model seemed confused.”

Retrieval-Augmented Tooling

RAG is not a monolith; it is a pipeline whose stages can each be formalized, measured, and improved.

Probabilistic formulation

For query context (x), retrieved document (d), and answer (y): [ p(y\mid x) = \sum_{d \in \mathcal{D}} p(y\mid x,d)\,p(d\mid x). ] Operationally, (p(d\mid x)) is retrieval/ranking, while (p(y\mid x,d)) is grounded generation. Agentic retrieval triggers should depend on uncertainty: [ \texttt{retrieve}_t = \mathbf{1}{H[p(\cdot\mid h_t)] > \tau}. ]

Three-theory braid

  1. Latent-document generation. RAG models combine parametric generation with non-parametric memory [14].
  2. Dense representation retrieval. DPR-style dual encoders formalize semantic nearest-neighbor access to large corpora [15].
  3. Classical IR ranking theory. Probabilistic ranking (e.g., BM25 family) provides robust lexical grounding and interpretable ranking signals [46].

How to study this formally

Measure retrieval nDCG/Recall@k, citation faithfulness, and end-task utility under retrieval budget constraints. Compare always-retrieve versus uncertainty-triggered retrieval policies. If retrieval cannot justify its latency with measurable uncertainty reduction, it is ritual, not reasoning.

Embodiment: Sensors, Actuators, and Feedback

Embodiment means the world can answer back. Even software-only agents are embodied in systems with latency, saturation, and irreversible side effects.

State-space formalization

Let continuous latent state (x_t), control (u_t), and observation (o_t): [ x_{t+1}=f(x_t,u_t)+w_t,\qquad o_t=g(x_t)+v_t. ] The controller chooses (u_t=\pi(o_{0:t},u_{0:t-1})) to optimize long-run utility under actuator and safety bounds.

Sensor quality enters through observability; actuator quality enters through controllability and delay.

Three-theory braid

  1. Control-theoretic state estimation. Kalman-style filtering formalizes noisy sensing and recursive belief updates [36].
  2. Reinforcement learning dynamics. MDP/POMDP and return optimization model delayed consequences of action [3] [4].
  3. System-level environment coupling. Agent loops embedded in real infrastructures require explicit modeling of latency, rate limits, and non-stationarity [2].

How to study this formally

Quantify sensor noise sensitivity, actuator saturation failures, and closed-loop stability under delays. Evaluate with perturbation tests and feedback-loop stress scenarios. An embodied agent that ignores feedback geometry is not autonomous; it is merely loud.

Safety Constraints and Guardrails

Safety is not a postscript to capability; it is constrained optimization from first principles.

Constrained control formalization

Model policy selection as a constrained MDP: [ \max_{\pi}\ J_R(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\pi!\left[\sum_t\gamma^t r_t\right] \quad\text{s.t.}\quad J}(\pi)=\mathbb{E\pi!\left[\sum_t\gamma^t c\right]\le d_j. ] The Lagrangian form [ \mathcal{L}(\pi,\lambda)=J_R(\pi)-\sum_j\lambda_j\big(J_{C_j}(\pi)-d_j\big) ] supports dual optimization and transparent trade-off tuning.

Three-theory braid

  1. Constrained MDP theory. Utility-safety trade-offs become explicit and optimizable [51].
  2. Control barrier functions (CBFs). Safety can be imposed as forward-invariance constraints (h(x)\ge0) at runtime [52].
  3. Normative governance frameworks. Constitutional and risk-management frameworks encode institution-level constraints beyond model internals [29] [53].

How to study this formally

Report Pareto fronts of task return versus violation probability, plus time-to-escalation under unsafe trajectories. Layered guardrails should be tested for correlated failure modes, not in isolation. Constraint-aware autonomy is not anti-innovation; it is innovation that survives contact with reality.

Coordination Protocols and Communication

In multi-agent systems, communication is not chatter; it is distributed computation under uncertainty and delay.

Formal protocol model

Let agents (i\in{1,\dots,n}) have local state (x_i^t) and messages (m_{i\to j}^t).
A protocol (\Pi) defines transition rules [ (x_i^{t+1}, m_{i\to }^{t+1}) = \Pi_i!\left(x_i^t,{m_{\to i}^t}\right). ] Correctness criteria include safety (nothing bad happens), liveness (something good eventually happens), and agreement/consistency when required.

Three-theory braid

  1. Distributed consensus limits. Byzantine agreement and impossibility results formalize what reliable coordination can and cannot guarantee [54] [55].
  2. Coordination theory. Task dependencies and resource constraints determine which communication structures are efficient [56].
  3. Role-based MAS architectures. Agent communication languages and protocol roles improve traceability and conflict handling [17] [18].

How to study this formally

Evaluate message complexity, consensus latency, deadlock frequency, and degradation under dropped/incorrect messages. Encode schemas and role permissions as enforceable protocol rules. If coordination depends on everyone being “reasonable,” it is not a protocol; it is a prayer.

Negotiation and Mechanism Design

Negotiation is what happens when autonomy meets scarcity. Mechanism design is how we stop that meeting from turning into chaos.

Formal mechanism frame

A mechanism is [ \mathcal{M}=(N,\Theta, A, g, p), ] with agents (N), types (\Theta), outcome space (A), allocation rule (g), and transfers (p).
Desired properties: incentive compatibility (IC), individual rationality (IR), and budget feasibility.

For truthful dominant-strategy reporting, each agent (i) should satisfy [ u_i!\big(g(\hat\theta_i,\hat\theta_{-i}),p_i(\hat\theta_i,\hat\theta_{-i});\theta_i\big) \ge u_i!\big(g(\theta'i,\hat\theta),p_i(\theta'i,\hat\theta);\theta_i\big). ]

Three-theory braid

  1. VCG-style efficient mechanisms. Transfer rules can align local truthfulness with global welfare [57] [58] [59].
  2. Social-choice limits. Gibbard-Satterthwaite impossibility reminds us that manipulation-free voting is highly constrained [60] [61].
  3. Contract-net negotiation. Task delegation via bidding provides practical distributed allocation under heterogeneous capabilities [62].

How to study this formally

Measure allocative efficiency, truthfulness regret, and fairness under strategic reporting. Simulate adversarial type misreports and collusion. A negotiation protocol without incentive analysis is merely an argument with extra JSON.

Equilibria, Self-Play, and Learning Dynamics

Equilibrium is the grammar of strategic stability: who can deviate, who gains, and when dynamics settle or cycle.

Formal game model

In a normal-form game ((N,{A_i},{u_i})), mixed strategy profile (\sigma^{}) is Nash if [ u_i(\sigma_i^{},\sigma_{-i}^{}) \ge u_i(\sigma_i,\sigma_{-i}^{})\quad \forall i,\forall \sigma_i. ] For sequential interaction, Markov games extend MDPs with multi-agent action tuples and payoff vectors.

Three-theory braid

  1. Nash equilibrium analysis. Fixed points characterize unilateral stability and expose incentive misalignment [19].
  2. Self-play in Markov games. Repeated interaction drives policy co-adaptation and emergent conventions [20] [21].
  3. Learning dynamics. Fictitious play and no-regret dynamics explain convergence to correlated/coarse-correlated equilibria in repeated games [65] [64] [63].

How to study this formally

Track exploitability, diversity collapse, and equilibrium selection under perturbation. Evaluate whether local agent improvements increase system-level welfare or merely shift failure to other roles. If strategic dynamics are ignored, “multi-agent” is just parallel monologue.

Neural Ensembles and Orchestration

An ensemble is a parliament of imperfect predictors. Its power comes from structured disagreement, not uniform certainty.

Formal aggregation model

Given predictors (f_k(x)), ensemble output is [ \hat{y}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k(x)\,f_k(x),\qquad \sum_k w_k(x)=1,\ w_k(x)\ge 0. ] For voting systems, (\hat{y}=\operatorname{mode}{f_k(x)}).
For MoE, router (g(x)) selects sparse experts (E(x)\subseteq{1,\dots,K}).

Generalization gain is tied to error covariance: diverse-but-competent experts beat correlated experts.

Three-theory braid

  1. Deep ensembles and uncertainty. Independent predictors improve calibration and robustness under shift [26] [67].
  2. Mixture-of-experts routing. Sparse specialization with learned gating yields scalable conditional computation [25] [68] [69].
  3. Orchestrated societies of specialists. Multi-agent compositions operationalize ensemble principles at workflow scale [23] [27].

How to study this formally

Measure ensemble gain versus best single expert, calibration under OOD inputs, and routing entropy (to detect expert collapse). The objective is not maximal committee size; it is minimal correlated error for a fixed budget.
